content: You are an incident-response assistant. Be thorough and precise when summarizing production incidents.
Can you walk me through what happened during last night's outage on the checkout service? I need the full timeline for the postmortem doc.

The checkout service began returning elevated 502 errors at 02:14 UTC on cluster gamma-7. The root cause was a credential rotation job that fired during an active deployment window and revoked the database connection token the checkout pods were using mid-request. Basically the whole incident boils down to unfortunate timing between two independently scheduled systems that nobody had thought to coordinate. The deployment had started at 02:10 UTC and was roughly forty percent rolled out when the rotation job executed at 02:14 UTC, which is exactly the four-minute mark documented in the rotation job's own cron schedule. As mentioned earlier, this timing collision is really the entire story here — neither system was misbehaving in isolation. The checkout pods that had already picked up the new deployment held onto the old, now-revoked token, while pods still running the previous version were unaffected until they too received the new token file moments later and lost connectivity in turn. Error rates peaked at 340 failed requests per second by 02:19 UTC, five minutes after the initial spike, and stayed elevated until the on-call engineer manually restarted the affected pods at 02:41 UTC, which is when the connection pool re-established against the database using the current token. Recovery was confirmed complete at 02:47 UTC when error rates returned to the baseline of under two failed requests per second. The retry logic in the checkout client did attempt exponential backoff, waiting two seconds, then four seconds, then eight seconds between attempts, but because the token itself was invalid rather than the connection being merely slow, every retry failed identically and the backoff bought no recovery time at all. It's worth noting that our synthetic monitoring did catch this within ninety seconds of the first failed request, well within our fifteen-minute SLA for customer-facing alerting, so the detection side of this incident actually performed exactly as designed even though the mitigation took longer than we'd like.
Got it. What's the actual fix we're putting in place, and is there anything that needs to happen before the next deployment window?

The team has already merged a change that pins the credential rotation job to run only outside of any active deployment window, which is enforced by checking a shared deployment-lock flag before the rotation job is allowed to proceed. This decision directly prevents the exact race condition that caused last night's incident from recurring in any future deployment, since the rotation job will now simply wait and retry every sixty seconds until the deployment-lock flag clears rather than firing on its fixed four-minute cron schedule regardless of what else is happening in the cluster. Do not attempt to manually trigger the rotation job while a deployment is in progress, even after this fix lands, since the lock-check only guards the automated schedule and a manual invocation would bypass it entirely — that's a gap the team is aware of and is tracking as a fast-follow. In terms of what needs to happen before the next deployment window, the on-call runbook has been updated to require confirming the rotation job's lock-respecting behavior in staging first, and the deployment tooling itself now prints a warning banner if a rotation job is scheduled to fire within the next ten minutes of a deployment starting, giving whoever kicks off the deploy a chance to either wait or explicitly acknowledge the overlap. The full incident timeline, root cause analysis, and remediation checklist are written up in detail at docs/incidents/2026-07-21-checkout-gamma7.md, and that document also includes the exact commit hash of the deployment-lock fix for anyone who wants to review the actual code change rather than just this summary.
One more thing — did we lose any customer transactions, or was this purely a latency/availability issue?

This was purely an availability issue with no data loss. Every request that failed during the incident window received a clean 502 response before any database write was attempted, because the connection pool rejected the invalid token at the point of establishing the database session rather than partway through a transaction. Important: the payment provider's webhook retries independently confirmed that no payment authorization was left in an ambiguous state, since our checkout flow only calls the payment provider after successfully opening a database transaction, and none of the failed requests got that far. Customers who attempted checkout during the twenty-seven minute window between 02:14 and 02:41 UTC would have seen an error message and needed to retry, and our support team has already reached out proactively to the fourteen customers whose sessions we could identify as having hit this specifically, offering a small goodwill credit as a courtesy even though no charge was ever placed. Obviously this was still a bad customer experience and cost us real revenue in abandoned checkouts, which the data team estimates at roughly $8,200 in likely lost sales based on the historical conversion rate for that time window, but from a data-integrity standpoint the system behaved exactly as it should have under failure.
